sections.title: Semaphore & BoundedSemaphore — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Q1: What is a Semaphore and how is it different from a Lock?

**✅ Answer:**
> "A Lock is a binary semaphore — it's either locked (0) or unlocked (1), allowing exactly one thread at a time. A Semaphore has a counter that can be N, allowing up to N threads to access the protected resource simultaneously.
>
> Conceptually: Lock = 1-slot parking lot, Semaphore = N-slot parking lot. When all slots are taken, new arrivals wait. When a car leaves, a waiting car enters.
>
> In practice: I use Lock for critical sections that must be serialized (incrementing a counter, updating shared state). I use Semaphore to implement resource pools (database connections, API rate limits, thread count limits). A connection pool allowing 10 simultaneous DB connections is a perfect Semaphore use case — more than 10 threads would wait until one finishes."

### Q2: When would you choose BoundedSemaphore over Semaphore?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Always in production code. `BoundedSemaphore` raises a `ValueError` if `release()` is called more times than `acquire()` — essentially preventing a `release()` bug from silently corrupting your semaphore's state.
>
> With a regular `Semaphore(3)`, if a bug causes an extra `release()`, the count goes to 4 — now 4 threads can enter simultaneously when only 3 should. This can cause subtle resource over-utilization that's hard to trace.
>
> With `BoundedSemaphore(3)`, the extra `release()` immediately raises `ValueError`, telling you exactly where the bug is. This is the 'fail fast' principle — better to crash loudly than corrupt data silently. I use `BoundedSemaphore` everywhere and only switch to `Semaphore` if I have a deliberate reason for the counter to exceed initial value (which is rare)."

### Q3: Can you implement a Lock using a Semaphore?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Yes — `Semaphore(1)` is functionally equivalent to a Lock:
> ```python
> lock_via_semaphore = threading.Semaphore(1)
> lock_via_semaphore.acquire()  # Lock
> # critical section
> lock_via_semaphore.release()  # Unlock
> ```
>
> However, there's an important difference: unlike `Lock`, a `Semaphore` can be released by a **different thread** than the one that acquired it. This makes Semaphores useful for **signaling between threads** (Thread A acquires, Thread B releases to signal completion), which you can't do with Lock.
>
> This signaling pattern is the basis of producer-consumer implementations. Actual `threading.Lock` is also slightly more efficient and provides ownership tracking, so for pure mutual exclusion, prefer Lock."

### Q4: What is the difference between a Semaphore and a Condition variable?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Both are synchronization primitives but for different use cases. A Semaphore is a simple counter — threads block when it hits zero and wake when it's incremented. It's stateless beyond the count.
>
> A `Condition` variable combines a Lock with wait/notify semantics. Threads can wait for an arbitrary condition to become true, and other threads notify them when state changes. Condition is more expressive — you can wait for 'buffer is not full AND my specific item type is available' rather than just 'any slot available.'
>
> I use Semaphore for capacity-limiting patterns (connection pools, rate limiting) where the count itself IS the condition. I use Condition for complex state-dependent waiting (wait until `buffer.size > 0 and buffer.has_priority_items()`)."

### Q5: How would you implement a thread pool using a Semaphore?

**✅ Answer:**
> "The Semaphore limits how many tasks run concurrently while allowing unlimited task submission:
> ```python
> class SimpleSemaphorePool:
>     def __init__(self, max_workers):
>         self._semaphore = threading.BoundedSemaphore(max_workers)
>
>     def submit(self, func, *args):
>         def run():
>             self._semaphore.acquire()
>             try:
>                 func(*args)
>             finally:
>                 self._semaphore.release()
>
>         t = threading.Thread(target=run)
>         t.start()
>         return t
>
> pool = SimpleSemaphorePool(max_workers=5)
> for i in range(20):
>     pool.submit(my_task, i)
> ```
>
> This creates one thread per task (20 threads) but only 5 run simultaneously — the others block on `acquire()`. The difference from `ThreadPoolExecutor` is that ThreadPoolExecutor reuses a fixed set of threads (better for many short tasks), while this approach creates a thread per task. For large task counts, ThreadPoolExecutor is more efficient — but this pattern is clean for understanding how pools work conceptually."

sections.title: Semaphore & BoundedSemaphore — Scenario-Based Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Scenario 1:
**"Your service makes calls to a third-party API that limits you to 10 concurrent requests. Exceeding this results in HTTP 429 errors. How do you implement this limit?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Textbook Semaphore use case:
> ```python
> import threading
> import requests
>
> class ThirdPartyAPIClient:
>     MAX_CONCURRENT = 10
>
>     def __init__(self):
>         self._semaphore = threading.BoundedSemaphore(self.MAX_CONCURRENT)
>         self._total_calls = 0
>         self._lock = threading.Lock()
>
>     def call(self, endpoint, params=None):
>         with self._semaphore:  # Blocks if 10 calls already in flight
>             with self._lock:
>                 self._total_calls += 1
>                 call_num = self._total_calls
>
>             try:
>                 response = requests.get(
>                     f'https://api.thirdparty.com{endpoint}',
>                     params=params,
>                     timeout=30
>                 )
>                 response.raise_for_status()
>                 return response.json()
>             except requests.HTTPError as e:
>                 if e.response.status_code == 429:
>                     # Shouldn't happen with semaphore, but handle gracefully
>                     time.sleep(1)
>                     raise
>
> client = ThirdPartyAPIClient()
> # Can be called from 100 threads simultaneously — max 10 will be in-flight
> ```
>
> In production, I'd also add retry logic with exponential backoff and jitter, plus monitoring on how often threads wait (high wait time = we're consistently at the limit and might need to negotiate a higher rate with the vendor)."

### Scenario 2:
**"Your image processing service converts images. Memory is limited — each conversion uses ~500MB and you have 4GB RAM. How do you prevent OOM crashes under high load?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "This is resource limiting by memory rather than connection count — still a Semaphore problem:
> ```python
> import threading
> import os
>
> AVAILABLE_RAM_GB = 4
> PER_CONVERSION_GB = 0.5
> MAX_CONCURRENT = int(AVAILABLE_RAM_GB / PER_CONVERSION_GB)  # = 8
>
> class ImageProcessor:
>     def __init__(self):
>         # Allow max 8 concurrent conversions (4GB / 0.5GB = 8)
>         self._memory_semaphore = threading.BoundedSemaphore(MAX_CONCURRENT)
>         self._stats = {'queued': 0, 'processing': 0, 'completed': 0}
>         self._stats_lock = threading.Lock()
>
>     def convert(self, image_path, output_format):
>         with self._stats_lock:
>             self._stats['queued'] += 1
>
>         # Block if memory is full — wait for a slot
>         with self._memory_semaphore:
>             with self._stats_lock:
>                 self._stats['queued'] -= 1
>                 self._stats['processing'] += 1
>             try:
>                 return self._do_convert(image_path, output_format)
>             finally:
>                 with self._stats_lock:
>                     self._stats['processing'] -= 1
>                     self._stats['completed'] += 1
>
>     def _do_convert(self, path, fmt):
>         # Actual conversion — uses ~500MB RAM
>         time.sleep(2)  # Simulate
>         return f"converted_{path}"
> ```
>
> This guarantees never more than 8 conversions in memory simultaneously. I'd also add a `timeout` parameter to the semaphore acquire and return HTTP 503 'Service Busy' if we wait too long, preventing the request queue from growing unboundedly."

### Scenario 3:
**"You have a web scraper that needs to respect politeness rules: max 3 concurrent requests to any single domain. How do you implement per-domain rate limiting?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Per-domain semaphores — a dict mapping domain to Semaphore:
> ```python
> import threading
> import re
> from urllib.parse import urlparse
>
> class PoliteScraper:
>     MAX_PER_DOMAIN = 3
>
>     def __init__(self):
>         self._domain_semaphores = {}
>         self._lock = threading.Lock()  # Protect the dict
>
>     def _get_semaphore(self, domain):
>         with self._lock:
>             if domain not in self._domain_semaphores:
>                 self._domain_semaphores[domain] = threading.BoundedSemaphore(
>                     self.MAX_PER_DOMAIN
>                 )
>             return self._domain_semaphores[domain]
>
>     def fetch(self, url):
>         domain = urlparse(url).netloc  # e.g., 'example.com'
>         semaphore = self._get_semaphore(domain)
>
>         with semaphore:  # Max 3 concurrent to this domain
>             print(f"Fetching {url} (domain: {domain})")
>             # response = requests.get(url, timeout=30)
>             time.sleep(random.uniform(0.5, 1.5))  # Simulate
>             return f"Content from {url}"
>
> scraper = PoliteScraper()
> urls = [
>     'https://site1.com/page1', 'https://site1.com/page2',
>     'https://site1.com/page3', 'https://site1.com/page4',  # 4th blocks
>     'https://site2.com/page1', 'https://site2.com/page2',  # Different domain — no wait!
> ]
>
> threads = [threading.Thread(target=scraper.fetch, args=(url,)) for url in urls]
> [t.start() for t in threads]
> [t.join() for t in threads]
> ```
>
> The key insight: site1's semaphore limits site1 concurrency without affecting site2. Each domain is independently rate-limited. I built this exact system for a competitor price monitoring tool — it prevented IP bans while still scraping 500+ sites concurrently."

sections.title: threading.Event — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Q1: What is `threading.Event` and what problem does it solve?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`threading.Event` is a thread synchronization primitive for **signaling between threads**. It wraps a boolean flag with thread-safe set/clear/wait operations. The core problem it solves: 'How does Thread A tell Thread B that something has happened?'
>
> Without Event, you'd poll a shared variable: `while not shared_flag: time.sleep(0.01)` — wasteful CPU usage. Event's `wait()` puts the thread to SLEEP (no CPU usage) until `set()` is called, then wakes ALL waiting threads simultaneously. This is efficient, clean, and correct.
>
> Real use cases: waiting for a service to initialize, signaling workers to stop, coordinating pipeline stages, and implementing one-time startup barriers."

### Q2: What is the difference between `event.wait()` and `event.wait(timeout=N)`?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`event.wait()` without timeout blocks **forever** until the event is set. This is risky in production — if the event never gets set (bug, crash of the signaling thread), the waiting thread hangs permanently.
>
> `event.wait(timeout=N)` returns `True` if the event was set within N seconds, or `False` if it timed out. This allows you to implement fallback behavior:
> ```python
> if event.wait(timeout=30):
>     proceed_normally()
> else:
>     log.error('Service did not become ready in 30s')
>     raise ServiceUnavailableError()
> ```
>
> In production, I always use timeout. It's the difference between a service that hangs silently on startup and one that fails fast with a clear error message."

### Q3: What happens when `event.set()` is called and multiple threads are waiting?

**✅ Answer:**
> "ALL waiting threads are woken up simultaneously — this is one of Event's key properties. It's a **broadcast signal**, not point-to-point. Every thread blocked on `event.wait()` at the moment `set()` is called will wake up.
>
> And critically: after `set()`, any thread that calls `event.wait()` in the FUTURE will NOT block — it returns immediately because the flag is True. This 'sticky' behavior is different from a Condition variable which can miss signals.
>
> This makes Event perfect for one-time signals like 'service is ready' or 'shutdown requested' — late-arriving threads don't miss the signal. If you want threads to block again, call `event.clear()` to reset it."

### Q4: How is `threading.Event` different from `threading.Condition`?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Event is simpler and covers the common case: 'wait for a flag to be set.' Condition is more powerful: 'wait until an arbitrary condition is true,' with precise control over who to notify.
>
> Key differences:
> - **Event**: simple boolean flag, `wait()` blocks until True, `set()` wakes ALL waiters
> - **Condition**: wraps a Lock, `wait()` releases lock and blocks, `notify()` wakes ONE waiter, `notify_all()` wakes ALL
>
> Use Event when: 'has X happened?' is sufficient (initialization complete, shutdown requested).
> Use Condition when: you need to wait for a complex state ('queue is not empty AND has high-priority items') and want to wake only specific threads.
>
> I reach for Event first — it's simpler and less error-prone. Only when I need notify() semantics or complex state-based waiting do I use Condition."

### Q5: Can you use `threading.Event` for repeated signaling?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Yes, by using `event.clear()` after each signal cycle. Set → waiters run → clear → set again → new waiters run. This is how you build a traffic light or checkpoint synchronization.
>
> But there's a subtle race condition: if you `clear()` right after `set()`, some threads might miss the signal:
> ```python
> event.set()    # Thread A sees it set, Thread B hasn't called wait() yet
> event.clear()  # Cleared before Thread B calls wait()!
> # Thread B now waits forever — it missed the signal!
> ```
>
> For repeated signaling where every thread must see every signal, use `threading.Barrier` (for synchronized bursts) or a `queue.Queue` with one item per thread (each gets its own message). Event is best for one-time signals or signals where missing the signal is acceptable (e.g., 'please check for new work' where checking again later is fine)."

sections.title: threading.Event — Scenario-Based Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
### Scenario 1:
**"You're building a microservice that needs to load configuration from an external service on startup. All incoming requests must be held until configuration is loaded. How do you implement this?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Perfect Event use case — a startup gate:
> ```python
> import threading
> import time
>
> class ConfigurableService:
>     def __init__(self):
>         self._config_loaded = threading.Event()
>         self._config = {}
>         self._load_failed = False
>         self._load_error = None
>
>         # Load config in background, don't block constructor
>         threading.Thread(target=self._load_config, daemon=True).start()
>
>     def _load_config(self):
>         try:
>             # Fetch from config service
>             config = fetch_config_from_consul()  # Takes 1-2s
>             self._config = config
>             self._config_loaded.set()  # ✅ Gate opens!
>         except Exception as e:
>             self._load_failed = True
>             self._load_error = e
>             self._config_loaded.set()  # Open gate even on failure
>
>     def handle_request(self, request):
>         # Block until config is ready (max 10 seconds)
>         if not self._config_loaded.wait(timeout=10):
>             return 503, 'Service starting up, please retry'
>
>         if self._load_failed:
>             return 500, f'Config load failed: {self._load_error}'
>
>         # Process request with config
>         return 200, process(request, self._config)
> ```
>
> This pattern was used in a Kubernetes service I deployed — pods start serving health checks (for readiness probes) immediately, but actual business requests block until config loads. The Event's sticky behavior means once config loads, all subsequent requests go through immediately with no overhead."

### Scenario 2:
**"You have a test suite where each test must wait for the previous test's cleanup to complete before starting. How do you coordinate this with Events?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Chain of Events — each test has a 'ready' event that the previous test sets:
> ```python
> class SequentialTestCoordinator:
>     def __init__(self, num_tests):
>         # Each test waits on previous test's done event
>         self._events = [threading.Event() for _ in range(num_tests + 1)]
>         self._events[0].set()  # First test can start immediately
>
>     def run_test(self, test_id, test_func):
>         # Wait for previous test to finish cleanup
>         print(f"Test {test_id}: Waiting for previous test cleanup...")
>         self._events[test_id - 1].wait()  # Wait for my 'start' signal
>
>         print(f"Test {test_id}: 🧪 Running test...")
>         try:
>             result = test_func()
>             print(f"Test {test_id}: ✅ Passed")
>         except AssertionError as e:
>             print(f"Test {test_id}: ❌ Failed: {e}")
>         finally:
>             # Cleanup
>             print(f"Test {test_id}: 🧹 Cleaning up...")
>             time.sleep(0.2)  # Simulate cleanup
>             self._events[test_id].set()  # Signal: next test can start!
>
> coordinator = SequentialTestCoordinator(5)
> test_functions = [lambda: time.sleep(0.3) for _ in range(5)]
>
> threads = [
>     threading.Thread(target=coordinator.run_test, args=(i+1, fn))
>     for i, fn in enumerate(test_functions)
> ]
> [t.start() for t in threads]
> [t.join() for t in threads]
> ```
>
> In CI systems I've worked on, this pattern ensures database tests run in isolation — each test waits for the previous one's DB cleanup before writing its own data."

### Scenario 3:
**"Your application has a 'maintenance mode' feature. When maintenance starts, new requests are blocked; when maintenance ends, all blocked requests resume. Design this."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "An Event that's normally SET (requests flow through) and temporarily CLEARED (requests block):
> ```python
> class MaintenanceModeMiddleware:
>     def __init__(self):
>         self._open_event = threading.Event()
>         self._open_event.set()  # Start in OPEN state (normal operation)
>         self._maintenance_reason = None
>
>     def enable_maintenance(self, reason="Scheduled maintenance"):
>         self._maintenance_reason = reason
>         self._open_event.clear()  # CLOSE: incoming requests will block
>         print(f"🔧 Maintenance mode ON: {reason}")
>         # In real system: drain existing requests first (wait for active count to reach 0)
>
>     def disable_maintenance(self):
>         self._maintenance_reason = None
>         self._open_event.set()   # OPEN: all blocked requests resume immediately!
>         print("✅ Maintenance mode OFF: all requests resuming")
>
>     def handle_request(self, request_id):
>         # Wait for maintenance to end (max 5 minutes)
>         if not self._open_event.wait(timeout=300):
>             return 503, 'Service in maintenance for too long'
>
>         if self._maintenance_reason:
>             # Safety check (race condition guard)
>             return 503, f'Maintenance: {self._maintenance_reason}'
>
>         # Normal request processing
>         return 200, f'Processed request {request_id}'
>
> middleware = MaintenanceModeMiddleware()
>
> def simulate_requests():
>     for i in range(10):
>         time.sleep(0.2)
>         status, body = middleware.handle_request(i)
>         print(f"  Request {i}: HTTP {status} — {body}")
>
> req_thread = threading.Thread(target=simulate_requests)
> req_thread.start()
>
> time.sleep(1)
> middleware.enable_maintenance('Database migration')
> time.sleep(2)  # Maintenance window
> middleware.disable_maintenance()
>
> req_thread.join()
> ```
>
> The `event.set()` in `disable_maintenance()` wakes ALL blocked threads simultaneously — no need to notify each one. In a high-traffic system, hundreds of queued requests can resume within milliseconds of maintenance ending."

sections.title: threading.Condition — Conceptual Interview Q&A
sections.body:
### Q1: Why must condition.wait() always be inside a while loop?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Two reasons: **spurious wakeups** and **multiple consumers**. Spurious wakeups are documented in POSIX — an OS can wake a waiting thread for no reason. Without a `while` loop, the thread would proceed even though the condition is still false.
>
> More commonly in Python: with multiple consumers, `notify()` wakes ONE thread. But by the time that thread re-acquires the lock, another consumer might have already consumed the data. Without `while`, the woken thread processes an empty structure.
>
> ```python
> # WRONG — check once, then trust it:
> with condition:
>     if not queue:
>         condition.wait()
>     item = queue.pop()  # queue might be empty again!
>
> # CORRECT — re-verify after every wakeup:
> with condition:
>     while not queue:
>         condition.wait()
>     item = queue.pop()  # Guaranteed non-empty
> ```
> This is so important that Python docs explicitly state: 'Always use wait() inside a while loop checking the condition.'"

### Q2: What is the difference between Condition.notify() and Condition.notify_all()?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`notify()` wakes exactly ONE thread from the waiters. Which one? It's OS-dependent — you can't choose. `notify_all()` wakes ALL waiting threads simultaneously.
>
> Use `notify()` when: exactly one thread can handle the event (e.g., one item was added to a queue — only one consumer should take it). More efficient.
>
> Use `notify_all()` when: all threads should re-evaluate their condition (e.g., multiple threads waiting for 'status == READY' — when status changes, all should check). Or when you're not sure which thread should run.
>
> In production I lean toward `notify_all()` for correctness — it's less efficient but never deadlocks from missing a notification. I optimize to `notify()` only when profiling shows contention."

### Q3: Why does Condition have a built-in Lock, and what is it for?

**✅ Answer:**
> "The Lock inside Condition serves two purposes: it protects the shared state you're checking, AND it ensures that checking the condition and calling `wait()` are atomic.
>
> Without this atomic guarantee, there's a race condition:
> ```
> Thread 1: checks 'is queue empty?' → YES
> Thread 2: adds item + calls notify() → but Thread 1 hasn't called wait() yet!
> Thread 1: calls wait() → waits FOREVER (missed the notify!)
> ```
>
> With the Condition lock, `wait()` atomically releases the lock AND starts waiting — no notification can slip through. When woken, it re-acquires the lock before returning. This is why you MUST call `notify()` and `wait()` inside `with condition:` — calling them outside raises `RuntimeError`."

### Q4: How is threading.Condition different from threading.Event?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Event is simpler — binary flag, all waiters wake on `set()`, no lock management. Condition is more powerful — wraps a lock, supports arbitrary predicate checking, granular `notify()` vs `notify_all()`.
>
> Key practical differences:
> - Event is 'sticky' — once set, future `wait()` calls return immediately. Condition's `wait()` always re-checks the while loop condition.
> - Event wakes ALL waiters always. Condition lets you wake ONE or ALL.
> - Condition requires you to manage the shared state manually (with the lock). Event IS the shared state.
>
> I use Event for simple on/off signals (shutdown requested, service ready). I use Condition for producer-consumer patterns where the waiting condition depends on complex mutable state."

### Q5: Can you use Condition without a Lock argument?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Yes, and this is the common usage. `threading.Condition()` creates its own internal `RLock` automatically. This internal lock is what `with condition:` acquires and what `wait()` releases/re-acquires.
>
> You pass an explicit lock only when multiple Conditions need to share the same lock, or when you need to coordinate a Condition with other lock-based operations on the same data:
> ```python
> shared_lock = threading.RLock()
> condition_a = threading.Condition(shared_lock)
> condition_b = threading.Condition(shared_lock)
> # Both conditions protect the same data under one lock
> ```
>
> If you pass a lock, it must be an `RLock` (not `Lock`) because `wait()` acquires it multiple times internally."

sections.title: threading.Condition — Scenario-Based Q&A
sections.body:
### Scenario 1:
**"Build a thread-safe bounded queue from scratch using Condition."**

**✅ Answer:**
```python
import threading

class BoundedQueue:
    def __init__(self, max_size):
        self._queue = []
        self._max = max_size
        self._condition = threading.Condition()

    def put(self, item, timeout=None):
        with self._condition:
            # Wait while full
            if timeout:
                import time
                deadline = time.time() + timeout
                while len(self._queue) >= self._max:
                    remaining = deadline - time.time()
                    if remaining <= 0:
                        raise queue.Full("Queue full, timeout exceeded")
                    self._condition.wait(timeout=remaining)
            else:
                while len(self._queue) >= self._max:
                    self._condition.wait()

            self._queue.append(item)
            self._condition.notify()  # Wake one consumer

    def get(self, timeout=None):
        with self._condition:
            while not self._queue:
                if timeout:
                    if not self._condition.wait(timeout=timeout):
                        raise queue.Empty("Queue empty, timeout exceeded")
                else:
                    self._condition.wait()
            item = self._queue.pop(0)
            self._condition.notify()  # Wake one producer
            return item

    def size(self):
        with self._condition:
            return len(self._queue)
```
> "This is essentially how Python's `queue.Queue` is implemented internally — built on top of `threading.Condition`."

### Scenario 2:
**"Multiple threads are waiting for a shared resource. When the resource becomes available, only the thread with highest priority should get it. How do you implement with Condition?"**

**✅ Answer:**
```python
import threading
import heapq

class PriorityResourceManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self._available = True
        self._waiters = []  # (priority, thread_id, event)
        self._lock = threading.Condition()
        self._counter = 0

    def acquire(self, priority=0):
        with self._lock:
            if self._available:
                self._available = False
                return  # Got it immediately

            # Add to priority queue
            event = threading.Event()
            heapq.heappush(self._waiters, (priority, self._counter, event))
            self._counter += 1

        # Wait outside lock
        event.wait()

    def release(self):
        with self._lock:
            if self._waiters:
                # Wake highest priority waiter
                _, _, event = heapq.heappop(self._waiters)
                event.set()  # Wake the specific waiter
            else:
                self._available = True
```
> "The key: use Condition to protect the waiters list, but individual `threading.Event` objects to wake specific threads. This gives precise control over which thread runs next."

### Scenario 3:
**"Your pipeline has stages where Stage 2 can only start when Stage 1 has processed at least 10 items. How do you implement this threshold-based coordination?"**

**✅ Answer:**
```python
import threading

class ThresholdPipeline:
    def __init__(self, threshold=10):
        self._buffer = []
        self._threshold = threshold
        self._condition = threading.Condition()
        self._stage1_done = False

    def stage1_produce(self, items):
        for item in items:
            processed = item * 2  # Some processing
            with self._condition:
                self._buffer.append(processed)
                print(f"  Stage1: produced item {processed} "
                      f"(buffer: {len(self._buffer)})")
                # Only notify when threshold reached OR all done
                if (len(self._buffer) >= self._threshold or
                        item == items[-1]):
                    self._condition.notify_all()
            time.sleep(0.1)

        with self._condition:
            self._stage1_done = True
            self._condition.notify_all()

    def stage2_consume(self):
        with self._condition:
            # Wait until buffer has at least threshold items
            while (len(self._buffer) < self._threshold
                   and not self._stage1_done):
                print(f"  Stage2: Waiting for {self._threshold} items "
                      f"(have {len(self._buffer)})...")
                self._condition.wait()

            items_to_process = self._buffer[:]
            self._buffer.clear()

        print(f"  Stage2: Processing {len(items_to_process)} items: "
              f"{items_to_process}")
```

sections.title: threading.Barrier — Conceptual Interview Q&A
sections.body:
### Q1: What is threading.Barrier and when would you use it?

**✅ Answer:**
> "A Barrier is a synchronization point where N threads all must arrive before any can continue. It's essentially a 'rendezvous' mechanism. Once the Nth thread arrives, all N are released simultaneously.
>
> I use Barriers for **phased parallel algorithms** where correctness requires that Phase 1 is 100% complete before Phase 2 starts, but you want maximum parallelism within each phase. Classic examples: parallel matrix multiplication (all row computations done before column pass), game engine updates (all physics calculated before rendering), distributed load testing (all test clients ready before traffic begins).
>
> The key difference from Event: Barrier auto-resets for the next use — it's designed for repeated synchronization points, not one-time signals."

### Q2: What is BrokenBarrierError and when does it occur?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`BrokenBarrierError` is raised when a barrier enters a 'broken' state, which happens when:
> 1. A thread calls `barrier.wait()` with a timeout and the timeout expires
> 2. A thread calls `barrier.abort()` explicitly
> 3. The `action` callback raises an exception
>
> Once broken, ALL threads currently waiting AND all future `wait()` calls raise `BrokenBarrierError` — the barrier is unusable. You must call `barrier.reset()` to restore it.
>
> In production, I always use `barrier.wait(timeout=N)` and handle `BrokenBarrierError` with graceful cleanup. A barrier timing out usually means one worker crashed or hung — you don't want the other N-1 workers waiting forever."

### Q3: What does the `action` parameter in Barrier do?

**✅ Answer:**
> "The `action` is a callable that runs exactly **once** when the last thread arrives at the barrier, **before** any thread is released. It's like a 'between phases' callback.
>
> ```python
> def log_phase_complete():
>     print(f'Phase {current_phase} done! Aggregating results...')
>     aggregate_results()  # Runs once, before all threads proceed
>
> barrier = threading.Barrier(N, action=log_phase_complete)
> ```
>
> The action runs in the context of the last thread to arrive. It's perfect for: saving intermediate results, logging phase completion, preparing data for the next phase, checking correctness before proceeding. If the action raises an exception, the barrier enters broken state."

### Q4: What is the return value of barrier.wait()?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`barrier.wait()` returns an integer from 0 to `parties-1` — the arrival position of each thread. The last thread to arrive (which triggers the release) gets 0. Earlier arrivals get 1, 2, etc. (or any ordering — it's not guaranteed to be strictly sequential, but one thread gets 0).
>
> This is useful for **electing a leader** — the thread that gets 0 does post-phase work:
> ```python
> position = barrier.wait()
> if position == 0:  # I'm the 'leader' for this phase
>     cleanup_from_previous_phase()
>     prepare_next_phase()
> # All threads then continue with next phase
> ```
> I've used this pattern in parallel algorithms where one thread needs to merge partial results before all threads proceed to the next computation step."

### Q5: How does Barrier differ from using multiple Events for synchronization?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Both can coordinate threads at checkpoints, but Barrier is specifically designed for the 'all must arrive before any proceed' pattern and handles it correctly with much less code.
>
> With Events, simulating a barrier manually requires:
> ```python
> # Manual barrier attempt — error-prone!
> arrived_count = 0
> all_arrived_event = threading.Event()
> count_lock = threading.Lock()
>
> def at_checkpoint():
>     global arrived_count
>     with count_lock:
>         arrived_count += 1
>         if arrived_count == N:
>             all_arrived_event.set()
>     all_arrived_event.wait()
>     # BUG: arrived_count not reset for next barrier!
> ```
> This has subtle bugs with reuse, thread safety, and reset logic. `threading.Barrier` handles all of this correctly, including auto-reset, broken state, timeouts, and the action callback. Always use the purpose-built primitive."

sections.title: threading.Barrier — Scenario-Based Q&A
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Barrier ensures all clients ready before ANY starts
- Phase 1: Setup — connect, authenticate, prepare
- ALL 50 clients wait here — fire together!
- Phase 2: Simultaneous load — all clients fire at once!
- Barrier: wait for all chunks to be sorted before merging
- Wait for ALL workers to finish sorting
- Only one worker (position 0) does the merge
- Simple merge of sorted arrays

**Defines:** `LoadTestCoordinator`, `parallel_merge_sort()`, `GameEngine`

### Scenario 1:
**"You're building a parallel load test. 50 clients must all start sending requests at exactly the same moment. How do you implement this?"**

**✅ Answer:**
```python
import threading
import time
import random

class LoadTestCoordinator:
    def __init__(self, num_clients):
        self.num_clients = num_clients
        # Barrier ensures all clients ready before ANY starts
        self.start_barrier = threading.Barrier(num_clients)
        self.results = []
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def run_client(self, client_id, target_url, num_requests):
        # Phase 1: Setup — connect, authenticate, prepare
        print(f"  Client {client_id:3d}: Connecting to {target_url}...")
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0.1, 0.5))  # Variable setup time
        print(f"  Client {client_id:3d}: Ready! "
              f"[{self.start_barrier.n_waiting + 1}/{self.num_clients} ready]")

        # ALL 50 clients wait here — fire together!
        self.start_barrier.wait()

        # Phase 2: Simultaneous load — all clients fire at once!
        print(f"  Client {client_id:3d}: 🔫 FIRING!")
        start = time.time()
        successes = 0
        for _ in range(num_requests):
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0.01, 0.05))  # Simulate request
            if random.random() > 0.05:  # 95% success rate
                successes += 1

        duration = time.time() - start
        with self._lock:
            self.results.append({
                'client': client_id,
                'successes': successes,
                'duration': duration,
                'rps': successes / duration
            })

coordinator = LoadTestCoordinator(num_clients=10)
threads = [
    threading.Thread(
        target=coordinator.run_client,
        args=(i+1, 'https://api.example.com', 20)
    ) for i in range(10)
]

print("=== Load Test: All 10 clients fire simultaneously ===\n")
[t.start() for t in threads]
[t.join() for t in threads]

total_rps = sum(r['rps'] for r in coordinator.results)
print(f"\n📊 Results: {total_rps:.1f} total RPS across all clients")
```

### Scenario 2:
**"You're implementing a parallel sorting algorithm. Multiple threads sort their chunks, then merge. How do you ensure merge doesn't start before all sorting is done?"**

**✅ Answer:**
```python
import threading
import random
import time

def parallel_merge_sort(data, num_workers=4):
    chunks = [[] for _ in range(num_workers)]
    chunk_size = len(data) // num_workers
    sorted_chunks = [None] * num_workers

    # Distribute data
    for i in range(num_workers):
        start = i * chunk_size
        end = start + chunk_size if i < num_workers - 1 else len(data)
        chunks[i] = data[start:end]

    # Barrier: wait for all chunks to be sorted before merging
    sort_barrier = threading.Barrier(num_workers)

    def sort_chunk(worker_id):
        print(f"  Worker {worker_id}: Sorting {len(chunks[worker_id])} items...")
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0.1, 0.5))  # Simulate sort time
        sorted_chunks[worker_id] = sorted(chunks[worker_id])
        print(f"  Worker {worker_id}: ✅ Sorted!")

        # Wait for ALL workers to finish sorting
        position = sort_barrier.wait()

        # Only one worker (position 0) does the merge
        if position == 0:
            print(f"\n  [Merger] All chunks sorted! Merging...")
            # Simple merge of sorted arrays
            result = []
            pointers = [0] * num_workers
            while True:
                available = [(sorted_chunks[i][pointers[i]], i)
                             for i in range(num_workers)
                             if pointers[i] < len(sorted_chunks[i])]
                if not available:
                    break
                min_val, min_i = min(available)
                result.append(min_val)
                pointers[min_i] += 1
            data[:] = result
            print(f"  [Merger] ✅ Merge complete!")

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=sort_chunk, args=(i,))
               for i in range(num_workers)]
    [t.start() for t in threads]
    [t.join() for t in threads]
    return data

data = [random.randint(1, 1000) for _ in range(40)]
print(f"Input (first 10): {data[:10]}")
result = parallel_merge_sort(data, num_workers=4)
print(f"Output (first 10): {result[:10]}")
print(f"Sorted correctly: {result == sorted(data)}")
```

### Scenario 3:
**"In a game engine, all game objects must update their position before any can render. How do you implement this game loop with Barrier?"**

**✅ Answer:**
```python
import threading
import time
import random

class GameEngine:
    def __init__(self, num_objects):
        self.num_objects = num_objects
        # 2-party barrier: update phase + render phase
        self.update_barrier = threading.Barrier(num_objects)
        self.render_barrier = threading.Barrier(num_objects)
        self.positions = {i: (0, 0) for i in range(num_objects)}
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self.frame = 0
        self.running = True

    def game_object(self, obj_id):
        while self.running:
            # PHASE 1: UPDATE — calculate new position
            new_x = random.randint(-10, 10)
            new_y = random.randint(-10, 10)
            with self._lock:
                self.positions[obj_id] = (new_x, new_y)

            # Wait for ALL objects to update before rendering
            pos = self.update_barrier.wait(timeout=2)
            if pos == 0:  # Leader increments frame
                self.frame += 1
                print(f"\n  🎮 Frame {self.frame}: All positions updated")

            # PHASE 2: RENDER — read positions (all safely updated now)
            with self._lock:
                pos = self.positions[obj_id]
            # print(f"  Object {obj_id}: rendering at {pos}")

            # Wait for ALL objects to finish rendering
            self.render_barrier.wait(timeout=2)

            if self.frame >= 5:
                self.running = False
                break

engine = GameEngine(num_objects=4)
threads = [threading.Thread(target=engine.game_object, args=(i,))
           for i in range(4)]
[t.start() for t in threads]
[t.join() for t in threads]
print(f"\n✅ Game loop ran {engine.frame} frames")
```

sections.title: threading.Timer — Conceptual Interview Q&A
sections.body:
### Q1: What is threading.Timer and how is it different from time.sleep()?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`threading.Timer` creates a NEW thread that waits N seconds then executes a function. The calling thread is NOT blocked — it continues executing immediately. `time.sleep()` blocks the CURRENT thread for N seconds — nothing else in that thread runs.
>
> The practical difference: with Timer, your main program continues running while waiting. You can start 100 different timers — they all count down independently in their own threads, none blocking others. `time.sleep(100)` would freeze your main thread for 100 seconds.
>
> I use Timer for async delayed callbacks (session timeout, retry logic), and `time.sleep()` when I explicitly want the current flow to pause (rate limiting, polling intervals)."

### Q2: Can you cancel a Timer after it has fired?

**✅ Answer:**
> "No. `cancel()` only works if the timer hasn't fired yet — if the timer is still in the waiting phase. Once the timer fires and starts executing its function, `cancel()` has no effect — the function runs to completion.
>
> ```python
> t = threading.Timer(0.001, important_func)  # Almost immediate
> t.start()
> time.sleep(1)  # Timer fires during this sleep
> t.cancel()     # No effect — function already ran!
> ```
>
> For cancellable in-flight operations, you need a threading.Event:
> ```python
> cancel_event = threading.Event()
> def cancellable_func():
>     if not cancel_event.is_set():
>         do_work()
> t = threading.Timer(5, cancellable_func)
> ```"

### Q3: How do you implement a repeating timer in Python?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Python's `Timer` is one-shot — it fires once. For repeating, reschedule inside the callback:
> ```python
> class RepeatingTimer:
>     def __init__(self, interval, func):
>         self._interval = interval
>         self._func = func
>         self._timer = None
>         self._running = False
>
>     def _run(self):
>         self._func()
>         if self._running:
>             self._timer = threading.Timer(self._interval, self._run)
>             self._timer.daemon = True
>             self._timer.start()
>
>     def start(self):
>         self._running = True
>         self._timer = threading.Timer(self._interval, self._run)
>         self._timer.daemon = True
>         self._timer.start()
>
>     def stop(self):
>         self._running = False
>         if self._timer:
>             self._timer.cancel()
> ```
> Note the drift issue: each timer starts AFTER the function completes, so actual interval = function_runtime + timer_interval. For precise timing, use `sched.scheduler` or APScheduler for production scheduling."

### Q4: What are the memory implications of using many Timer threads?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Each `threading.Timer` creates a full OS thread — with stack memory (~8MB default on Linux) and OS-level overhead. Creating thousands of timers = thousands of threads = gigabytes of memory.
>
> I've seen this become a serious issue in session management code that created one Timer per user session — with 50,000 concurrent users, that's 50,000 threads and ~400GB of stack allocation (even if not all committed).
>
> The production solution: use a **single background thread with a sorted heap of (fire_time, callback) tuples** — this is how `sched.scheduler` works. Or use APScheduler/Celery Beat for heavy scheduling workloads. For Python web frameworks, use task queues (Celery) rather than Timer threads for any deferred work."

### Q5: Is threading.Timer thread-safe?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`cancel()` is thread-safe — you can call it from any thread. Starting the timer (`start()`) and the callback execution are thread-safe in that sense too.
>
> But the pattern around Timer often introduces race conditions. Classic example: the 'cancel and reschedule' pattern:
> ```python
> # RACE CONDITION:
> if self._timer:
>     self._timer.cancel()   # Thread A cancels
>     # Thread B sees self._timer = old timer here!
> self._timer = threading.Timer(5, callback)  # Thread A sets new timer
> ```
> Thread B might cancel the NEW timer if it runs between the assignment and the cancel.
>
> Fix: protect the cancel-and-reschedule with a Lock:
> ```python
> with self._lock:
>     if self._timer: self._timer.cancel()
>     self._timer = threading.Timer(5, callback)
>     self._timer.start()
> ```
> I always use a Lock around any Timer cancel/reschedule — the timer itself is safe, but the surrounding logic often isn't."

sections.title: threading.Timer — Scenario-Based Q&A
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Decorator: only call function after wait_seconds of no new calls
- Simulate rapid typing — only last call within 0.3s should fire
- Output: Only ONE search fires — for 'python'
- Cancel existing timer for this key

**Defines:** `debounce()`, `search()`, `RetryWithBackoff`, `flaky_api_call()`, `TTLCache`

### Scenario 1: **"Build a debounce decorator for a search function."**

**✅ Answer:**
```python
import threading
import time

def debounce(wait_seconds):
    """Decorator: only call function after wait_seconds of no new calls"""
    def decorator(func):
        timer = [None]
        lock = threading.Lock()

        def debounced(*args, **kwargs):
            with lock:
                if timer[0]:
                    timer[0].cancel()
                timer[0] = threading.Timer(wait_seconds, func, args=args, kwargs=kwargs)
                timer[0].daemon = True
                timer[0].start()

        return debounced
    return decorator

@debounce(wait_seconds=0.3)
def search(query):
    print(f"  🔍 Searching for: '{query}'")

# Simulate rapid typing — only last call within 0.3s should fire
print("Simulating rapid typing 'p', 'py', 'pyt', 'pyth', 'python':")
search("p")
time.sleep(0.1)
search("py")
time.sleep(0.1)
search("pyt")
time.sleep(0.1)
search("pyth")
time.sleep(0.1)
search("python")
time.sleep(0.5)  # Wait for debounce to fire

# Output: Only ONE search fires — for 'python'
```

### Scenario 2: **"Implement retry with exponential backoff using Timer."**

**✅ Answer:**
```python
import threading
import time
import random

class RetryWithBackoff:
    def __init__(self, max_retries=5, base_delay=1.0, max_delay=30.0):
        self.max_retries = max_retries
        self.base_delay = base_delay
        self.max_delay = max_delay
        self._result_event = threading.Event()
        self._result = None
        self._error = None

    def _attempt(self, func, args, kwargs, attempt_num):
        try:
            self._result = func(*args, **kwargs)
            self._result_event.set()  # Success!
        except Exception as e:
            if attempt_num >= self.max_retries:
                self._error = e
                self._result_event.set()  # Give up
            else:
                delay = min(self.base_delay * (2 ** attempt_num)
                           + random.uniform(0, 1),  # Jitter
                           self.max_delay)
                print(f"  Attempt {attempt_num+1} failed: {e}. "
                      f"Retrying in {delay:.1f}s...")
                t = threading.Timer(delay, self._attempt,
                                    args=[func, args, kwargs, attempt_num + 1])
                t.daemon = True
                t.start()

    def execute(self, func, *args, **kwargs):
        self._attempt(func, args, kwargs, attempt_num=0)
        self._result_event.wait()  # Block until success or all retries exhausted
        if self._error:
            raise self._error
        return self._result

# Test
attempts = [0]
def flaky_api_call():
    attempts[0] += 1
    print(f"  📡 API call attempt #{attempts[0]}")
    if attempts[0] < 3:
        raise ConnectionError(f"Server busy (attempt {attempts[0]})")
    return {"data": "success!", "attempt": attempts[0]}

retry = RetryWithBackoff(max_retries=5, base_delay=0.5)
result = retry.execute(flaky_api_call)
print(f"  ✅ Final result: {result}")
```

### Scenario 3: **"Implement a cache with TTL (time-to-live) per entry."**

**✅ Answer:**
```python
import threading
import time

class TTLCache:
    def __init__(self):
        self._cache = {}
        self._timers = {}
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def set(self, key, value, ttl_seconds):
        with self._lock:
            # Cancel existing timer for this key
            if key in self._timers:
                self._timers[key].cancel()
            self._cache[key] = value

            # Schedule expiration
            timer = threading.Timer(ttl_seconds, self._expire, args=[key])
            timer.daemon = True
            timer.start()
            self._timers[key] = timer
        print(f"  Cache SET '{key}' = {value} (expires in {ttl_seconds}s)")

    def get(self, key):
        with self._lock:
            value = self._cache.get(key)
        if value is None:
            print(f"  Cache MISS for '{key}'")
        else:
            print(f"  Cache HIT: '{key}' = {value}")
        return value

    def _expire(self, key):
        with self._lock:
            self._cache.pop(key, None)
            self._timers.pop(key, None)
        print(f"  ⏰ Cache EXPIRED: '{key}'")

cache = TTLCache()
cache.set("user:1", {"name": "Alice"}, ttl_seconds=2)
cache.set("user:2", {"name": "Bob"},   ttl_seconds=4)
cache.set("config", {"theme": "dark"}, ttl_seconds=1)

time.sleep(0.5); cache.get("user:1")    # HIT
time.sleep(0.5); cache.get("config")    # Should MISS (expired at 1s)
time.sleep(0.5); cache.get("user:1")    # Should MISS (expired at 2s)
time.sleep(2.0); cache.get("user:2")    # Should MISS (expired at 4s)
```

sections.title: Thread-Local Data — Conceptual Interview Q&A
sections.body:
### Q1: What is threading.local() and what problem does it solve?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`threading.local()` creates objects where each thread has its own isolated namespace for attributes. The problem it solves: **sharing an object handle across threads while keeping per-thread state private**.
>
> Classic example: a Flask app stores the current HTTP request in `flask.g` (which uses thread-local storage). Hundreds of concurrent requests each need `g.user` to contain THEIR user, not someone else's. Without thread-local, you'd need to pass the request context to every single function — thread-local provides implicit per-thread context.
>
> The key insight: `threading.local()` doesn't prevent sharing — it makes the sharing transparent. The same `local` object is accessible everywhere, but `local.attribute` means different things in different threads."

### Q2: What happens when you access a thread-local attribute that hasn't been set in the current thread?

**✅ Answer:**
> "You get an `AttributeError` — the attribute doesn't exist in the current thread's namespace. This is different from a regular object where the attribute would exist globally.
>
> ```python
> local = threading.local()
> local.x = 10  # Set in main thread
>
> def worker():
>     print(local.x)  # AttributeError! Not set in this thread's namespace
> ```
>
> Best practice: always use `getattr` with a default:
> ```python
> user = getattr(thread_local, 'current_user', None)
> if user is None:
>     raise RuntimeError('No user context set for this thread')
> ```
>
> Or initialize in thread setup (like a web framework's request middleware does before calling user code)."

### Q3: Is threading.local() thread-safe?

**✅ Answer:**
> "The storage mechanism itself is thread-safe — Python ensures that accessing `local.attr` in Thread 1 and `local.attr` in Thread 2 are completely independent. No locks needed for the thread-local access itself.
>
> However, if a thread-local value holds a reference to a SHARED mutable object, that shared object is NOT thread-safe:
> ```python
> shared_list = [1, 2, 3]
> local.data = shared_list  # Thread-local reference to SHARED list!
>
> # Thread 1: local.data.append(4)  ← UNSAFE! Modifies shared_list!
> # Thread 2: local.data.append(5)  ← UNSAFE! Race condition!
> ```
>
> Thread-local protects the reference (`local.data = ...`), not the object it points to. Always use thread-local with per-thread COPIES of mutable data, not shared references."

### Q4: How does threading.local() work internally?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Internally, `threading.local()` uses the current thread's identity (`threading.get_ident()`) as a dictionary key. The local object has a main dict mapping `{thread_id: {attribute_name: value}}`.
>
> When you do `local.x = 10` in Thread 1: it stores `{thread1_id: {'x': 10}}`.
> When Thread 2 does `local.x = 20`: it stores `{thread2_id: {'x': 20}}`.
> Thread 1's `local.x` lookup: finds `thread1_id` → `{'x': 10}` → returns 10.
>
> When a thread dies, Python's cleanup removes that thread's entries from the local's dict — so thread-local values are GC'd properly when threads end. This is also why you shouldn't hold expensive resources in thread-local without explicit cleanup."

### Q5: When would you choose threading.local() over passing context as function arguments?

**✅ Answer:**
> "The trade-off is **implicit vs explicit** context.
>
> **Pass as arguments** (explicit): cleaner for simple call chains, easier to test, easier to reason about. Preferred in functional code.
>
> **thread-local** (implicit): cleaner when context needs to flow through many layers without touching every function signature. Essential when you can't modify intermediate function signatures (third-party libraries, decorators, middleware).
>
> Web frameworks use thread-local because the call chain is: web framework → middleware → your view → your helper → database layer — and passing request context through ALL of these would be unmanageable. Thread-local lets any layer access `current_user` without the entire chain needing to pass it.
>
> My rule: for new code, prefer explicit arguments for testability. Use thread-local for cross-cutting concerns (auth, logging, tracing) that span many layers, especially in framework-style code."

sections.title: Thread Communication — queue.Queue — Conceptual Interview Q&A
sections.body:
### Q1: Why use queue.Queue instead of a list with a Lock?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`queue.Queue` is the recommended thread-safe communication channel for threads. It handles all the complexity internally: locking, condition variables for blocking on empty/full, task completion tracking. Implementing this correctly with a list + Lock is tedious and error-prone.
>
> Specific advantages: `Queue.get()` blocks until data arrives (no busy polling), `Queue.put()` blocks if full (natural backpressure), `task_done()` + `join()` lets you wait for ALL work to be processed (not just dequeued), and the implementation is well-tested and optimized.
>
> I've seen teams roll their own queue with a Lock and a list, then spend days debugging edge cases around empty/full blocking. Queue solves all of it out of the box."

### Q2: What is the difference between queue.get() timing out and queue being empty?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`get(timeout=5)` returns an item if one becomes available within 5 seconds — it's time-bounded blocking. If no item arrives in 5 seconds, it raises `queue.Empty`.
>
> `get(block=False)` (equivalent to `get_nowait()`) raises `queue.Empty` IMMEDIATELY if the queue is currently empty — no waiting at all.
>
> `empty()` method is unreliable in multithreaded code — the queue might be empty when you check but have an item added before you call `get()`. The proper pattern is to call `get()` with a timeout and handle `queue.Empty`, rather than checking `empty()` first (that would be a TOCTOU race condition)."

### Q3: What is the Poison Pill pattern and when do you use it?

**✅ Answer:**
> "The Poison Pill is a sentinel value (usually `None` or a unique sentinel object) that signals a consumer thread to stop. You put N poison pills for N workers to gracefully stop them.
>
> ```python
> STOP = object()  # Unique sentinel
>
> for _ in range(num_workers):
>     queue.put(STOP)  # One pill per worker
>
> def worker():
>     while True:
>         item = queue.get()
>         if item is STOP:  # Use 'is' not '==' for sentinel!
>             break
>         process(item)
> ```
>
> I use it when: workers run until explicitly told to stop (not a fixed number of items). It's cleaner than `threading.Event` for queue-based workers because the stop signal flows through the same queue as work — preserving ordering. Alternative: use a separate stop Event and check it in the get() loop."

### Q4: Explain task_done() and queue.join(). When and why do you use them?

**✅ Answer:**
> "Queue maintains an internal counter of 'unfinished tasks' — incremented on every `put()`, decremented on every `task_done()`. `queue.join()` blocks until this counter reaches zero — meaning every item that was put() has been processed (not just dequeued).
>
> This matters because `get()` removes an item from the queue immediately, but the worker might still be processing it. Without `task_done()`, you can't know when ALL processing is complete.
>
> ```python
> q.put(item1)  # counter = 1
> q.put(item2)  # counter = 2
>
> item = q.get()  # counter still = 2! (dequeued but not processed)
> # ... process item ...
> q.task_done()   # counter = 1
>
> item = q.get()  # counter still = 1
> # ... process item ...
> q.task_done()   # counter = 0 → q.join() unblocks!
> ```
>
> Pattern: put all work, `queue.join()` in main thread, workers call `task_done()` after each item. This is like `Promise.all()` for thread work."

### Q5: When would you use LifoQueue or PriorityQueue over regular Queue?

**✅ Answer:**
> "`Queue` (FIFO) for most work queues — fair, preserves submission order. Good for request processing, download queues.
>
> `LifoQueue` (stack/LIFO): useful when recently submitted work is more likely to be relevant (cache locality). For example, a recently viewed page is more likely to be needed again than one viewed an hour ago. Web crawlers sometimes use LIFO for depth-first traversal.
>
> `PriorityQueue`: when items have different urgencies. `(priority, item)` tuples, lowest number = highest priority. Use cases: task schedulers (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW), network packets (QoS), customer service queues (premium vs standard support). Note: PriorityQueue is slower than Queue because it maintains heap order (O(log n) put/get vs O(1) for Queue). Use it only when priority ordering is genuinely needed."
